cim: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Cervical Cytology Screening Lacks Rigorous Clinical Validation
cim_eredeti: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Cervical Cytology Screening Lacks Rigorous Clinical Validation
szoveg_eredeti:
Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Cervical Cytology Screening Lacks Rigorous Clinical Validation

A comprehensive systematic review synthesizing research on explainable artificial intelligence applied to Pap smear and cervical cytology imaging has found that while technical investigations are expanding rapidly, rigorous clinical validation remains scarce across the field. Published in Frontiers in Systems Biology, the investigation analyzed 73 eligible studies published between January 2019 and March 2026 to assess how interpretability tools are implemented and evaluated in cervical cancer screening. The international research team discovered that despite the widespread display of visually intuitive heatmaps and localization outputs, fewer than one in ten studies formally verified whether these visual explanations genuinely reflect the internal reasoning driving deep learning predictions. This substantial imbalance between superficial visual plausibility and verifiable algorithmic transparency underscores a critical translational bottleneck that currently limits the safe integration of computational cytology platforms into routine clinical practice.

Cervical cancer represents a severe global health burden, standing as the fourth most common cancer among women globally with an estimated 660,000 incident cases and 350,000 deaths reported in 2022 by the World Health Organization. Cytology-based screening using conventional Pap smears or liquid-based preparations has long served as a cornerstone of preventive oncology by detecting identifiable precancerous lesions before invasive transformation occurs. However, manual cytological examination is notoriously labor-intensive, requiring trained human observers to inspect tens of thousands of normal or inflammatory cells on a glass slide to locate rare, microscopic abnormalities. The advent of whole-slide imaging and digital cytology prompted computer scientists to develop artificial intelligence models capable of automated cell classification, nucleus and cytoplasm segmentation, and lesion triage according to the standardized Bethesda System. Nevertheless, deep learning models frequently function as opaque black boxes, generating highly accurate classifications without exposing their internal logic to reviewing clinicians.

To investigate the extent to which explainable artificial intelligence resolves this interpretability challenge, the review authors executed a structured search across six electronic indexing databases—PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink—supplemented by citation tracking. Prospective registration was established through PROSPERO under identifier CRD420261419902, adhering strictly to the PRISMA 2020 reporting standards. Across the 73 included studies, publication dates demonstrated an exponential acceleration in research activity, with 56 studies, or 76.7 percent of the entire evidence base, appearing from 2024 onward, while only 17 studies were published between 2019 and 2023. All 73 investigations evaluated two-dimensional digital cytology imagery, ranging from cropped single-cell image patches to high-resolution whole-slide scans. Methodological quality and risk of bias were independently evaluated by two reviewers using QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy designs and PROBAST for prediction modeling, achieving an inter-reviewer agreement Cohen’s kappa of 0.835, indicating almost perfect consensus.

The review revealed substantial dependencies on isolated and unrepresentative data repositories across the published literature. Publicly accessible datasets supported model development and testing in 41 studies, representing 56.2 percent of the analyzed corpus, whereas private or institutional clinical datasets were utilized in 29 studies, or 39.7 percent. A remaining three investigations, accounting for 4.1 percent, relied on mixed or unclear data sources. Crucially, external validation against independent patient cohorts or separate scanning environments was reported in only 17 studies, or 23.3 percent, leaving 56 studies completely lacking external validation. Furthermore, multicenter data acquisition was present in only 21 studies, representing 28.8 percent, while 52 investigations depended strictly on single-center datasets or omitted institutional sampling details. Because external validation and multicenter enrollment were evaluated as separate methodological parameters, the data establish that the overwhelming majority of computational cytology pipelines remain validated solely within the precise archival conditions under which they were trained.

Across the examined architectures, convolutional neural networks served as the primary algorithmic backbone, complemented by emerging vision transformers, attention-augmented frameworks, graph neural networks, and classical machine learning classifiers. These models addressed diverse analytical objectives, including abnormal cell detection, nucleus segmentation, overlapping cell separation, and Bethesda-aligned case triaging. In parallel, researchers implemented a heterogeneous collection of explainability mechanisms. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping, known as Grad-CAM, emerged as the most prevalent individual method, utilized in 12 studies, representing 16.4 percent of the sample. Additional applied approaches included original Class Activation Mapping variants, raw saliency maps, integrated gradients, attention visualization matrices, local feature-importance scores, and segmentation-derived visual overlays. The synthesis highlighted that the cytology domain has not coalesced around a unified explainability framework, relying instead on varied techniques tailored to highlight localized microscopic structures.

Despite the diversity of technical approaches, the systematic synthesis uncovered significant methodological deficits in how generated explanations are formally verified. Overall explanation evaluation was categorized into three mutually exclusive strata: 42 studies, or 57.5 percent, relied entirely on qualitative visual inspection; 28 studies, or 38.4 percent, conducted formal or semi-formal evaluative assessments; and three studies, or 4.1 percent, reported no structured evaluation whatsoever. When investigators examined individual evaluation components across all 73 studies, spatial localization was documented in 59 studies, representing 80.8 percent. In sharp contrast, explanation faithfulness was systematically tested in only six studies, or 8.2 percent, revealing a profound 72.6 percentage point disparity between spatial localization and mechanistic verification. This contrast indicates that while authors routinely demonstrated that heatmaps overlap with visual abnormalities, they rarely tested whether model predictions were causally dependent on those highlighted regions.

Human-centered clinical evaluation was similarly underrepresented across the systematic evidence base. Formal clinician review of generated explanations occurred in only 20 studies, or 27.4 percent, while 53 studies omitted expert clinician evaluation entirely. Structured reader studies comparing diagnostic accuracy with and without algorithmic assistance were conducted in 15 investigations, representing 20.5 percent of the literature. Furthermore, objective usability testing was reported in only 17 studies, or 23.3 percent, and direct assessments of clinician trust, confidence, or willingness to rely on system outputs were identified in just nine studies, representing 12.3 percent. The authors emphasized that expert participation, visual plausibility, or localization agreement cannot serve as clinical proxies for genuine clinician trust or algorithmic faithfulness.
